facts.title: Named For Berkeley
facts.text: Berkelium was named after the city of Berkeley, California, home of the University of California laboratory where it was created. The naming deliberately echoes terbium, the element named after the Swedish village of Ytterby, because berkelium sits directly below terbium on the periodic table. The team noted the parallel openly, paying homage to the periodic table's vertical relationships.

facts.title: Born From A Cyclotron
facts.text: Berkelium was first synthesized in December 1949 by Glenn Seaborg, Stanley Thompson, and Albert Ghiorso. They bombarded a tiny sample of americium-241 with accelerated alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron at Berkeley, producing berkelium-243. It was the fifth transuranium element ever discovered.

facts.title: You Can't Find It In Nature
facts.text: Berkelium does not occur naturally on Earth in any measurable amount, because all of its isotopes are radioactive and decay far faster than the age of our planet. Every atom of berkelium that exists has been made artificially in reactors or accelerators. Trace amounts were once spread globally by atmospheric nuclear weapons testing in the 20th century, but these have long since decayed.

facts.title: A Metal You Could Hold (Briefly)
facts.text: Berkelium is a silvery, soft metal that is malleable enough to be shaped, and it is dense at about 14.8 grams per cubic centimeter. It melts at roughly 986 degrees Celsius. Despite these tangible metallic properties, only microgram-to-milligram quantities have ever been produced, so no one has ever forged a visible lump of it for everyday handling.

facts.title: It Glows With Its Own Heat
facts.text: The most stable isotope, berkelium-247, has a half-life of about 1,380 years, but the isotope usually produced, berkelium-249, lasts only around 330 days. Berkelium-249's radioactivity is so intense that samples warm themselves and emit a faint glow. This self-heating also slowly damages the element's own crystal structure from within as it decays.

facts.title: The Key To Element 117
facts.text: Berkelium's most famous practical role was as a target for making tennessine, element 117. In 2009 Oak Ridge National Laboratory produced about 22 milligrams of berkelium-249 over roughly a year, then shipped it to Russia. There, scientists bombarded it with calcium-48 ions to create the first atoms of tennessine in 2010.

facts.title: A Race Against Radioactive Decay
facts.text: Because berkelium-249 decays with a half-life of under a year, experiments using it are a race against time. The Oak Ridge berkelium shipped for the tennessine experiment was losing usable material every single day. Scientists had to carefully schedule the international transport and the irradiation to finish before too much of the precious target vanished.

facts.title: Hard To Make, Rarely Made
facts.text: Berkelium is one of the rarest synthetic elements, produced only at a handful of facilities such as Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor. Making it requires bombarding curium or plutonium targets with neutrons for long periods, building up heavier nuclei step by step. The world's total production has historically amounted to only a fraction of a gram at a time.

facts.title: It Likes To Be +3
facts.text: In chemical compounds berkelium most commonly adopts the +3 oxidation state, behaving much like other actinides and the lanthanide terbium above it. However, it can also reach an unusually accessible +4 state, which is rarer among the heavier actinides. This +4 chemistry helps chemists separate and purify berkelium from neighboring elements.

facts.title: Purely A Tool For Science
facts.text: Berkelium has no biological role and no commercial or medical uses; it is too scarce, too costly, and too radioactive to be practical for anything outside research. Its entire value lies in fundamental science, especially as a stepping-stone to forge superheavy elements at the very edge of the periodic table. Studying its bonding and electron behavior also tests our theories of how relativity reshapes the chemistry of heavy atoms.
